message.content: {"recommended_method":"social_choice","consensus_potential":0.55,"fairness_assessment":"A comparative vote with explicit criteria would fairly balance access, inclusion, feasibility, and long-term costs; an equal split should not be assumed fair if it underfunds both services.","conflict_severity":"medium","stakeholder_analysis":[{"agent":"agent_1","position":"Favors option A: expanding the children’s book collection, emphasizing traditional library use and youth access, but faces concerns about excluding users needing digital tools.","influence":0.33},{"agent":"agent_2","position":"Favors option B: creating a freely accessible digital space, emphasizing digital inclusion, but must address maintenance, connectivity, equipment renewal, and user support costs.","influence":0.33},{"agent":"agent_3","position":"Favors option C: dividing the grant equally between books and digital access, seeking balance but risking two underfunded and ineffective services.","influence":0.34}],"recommended_resolution":"collaborative","governance_reasoning":"Because the debate is evenly divided and each option has credible benefits and drawbacks, stakeholders should collaboratively define minimum viable funding, assess lifecycle costs and community needs, and then use a ranked social-choice vote. This avoids imposing a simplistic compromise while preserving procedural fairness."}
